claim: PIE-1 localizes to the germline in early C. elegans embryos where it prevents somatic differentiation programs.
source: In early Caenorhabditis elegans embryos, the CCCH zinc finger protein PIE-1 localizes to the germline where it prevents somatic differentiation programs.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known function of PIE-1.

claim: PIE-1 functions in the meiotic ovary where it becomes SUMOylated.
source: Here, we show that PIE-1 also functions in the meiotic ovary where it becomes SUMOylated and engages the small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO)-conjugating machinery.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: PIE-1 engages the SUMO-conjugating machinery in the meiotic ovary.
source: Here, we show that PIE-1 also functions in the meiotic ovary where it becomes SUMOylated and engages the small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO)-conjugating machinery.
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid data showing PIE-1 interacts with UBC-9 and other SUMO pathway components (Figure 1A).

claim: HDAC SUMOylation is a target of PIE-1 as identified by whole-SUMO-proteome mass spectrometry.
source: Using whole-SUMO-proteome mass spectrometry, we identify HDAC SUMOylation as a target of PIE-1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by mass spectrometry and western blot data in Figure 3.

claim: PIE-1 engages the SUMO machinery to preserve the germline fate in the embryo.
source: Our analyses of genetic interactions between pie-1 and SUMO pathway mutants suggest that PIE-1 engages the SUMO machinery both to preserve the germline fate in the embryo and to promote Argonaute-mediated surveillance in the adult germline.
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 2.

claim: PIE-1 engages the SUMO machinery to promote Argonaute-mediated surveillance in the adult germline.
source: Our analyses of genetic interactions between pie-1 and SUMO pathway mutants suggest that PIE-1 engages the SUMO machinery both to preserve the germline fate in the embryo and to promote Argonaute-mediated surveillance in the adult germline.
evidence: This is supported by piRNA sensor desilencing data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The C. elegans zygote P0 undergoes a series of asymmetric divisions that generate four somatic founder cells and the germline blastomere P4.
source: The C. elegans zygote, P0, undergoes a series of asymmetric divisions that generate four somatic founder cells and the germline blastomere P4.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: PIE-1 protein is maternally deposited and uniformly present in the cytoplasm and nucleus of the zygote.
source: The PIE-1 protein is maternally deposited and uniformly present in the cytoplasm and nucleus of the zygote, but rapidly disappears in each somatic blastomere shortly after division (Mello et al., 1996; Reese et al., 2000; Tenenhaus et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PIE-1 rapidly disappears in each somatic blastomere shortly after division.
source: The PIE-1 protein is maternally deposited and uniformly present in the cytoplasm and nucleus of the zygote, but rapidly disappears in each somatic blastomere shortly after division (Mello et al., 1996; Reese et al., 2000; Tenenhaus et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In pie-1 mutants, the germline lineage differentiates into extra intestinal cells causing an embryonic arrest.
source: In pie-1 mutants, the germline lineage differentiates into extra intestinal cells causing an embryonic arrest (Mello et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: PIE-1 localizes prominently in nuclei in the early P-lineage blastomeres and persists in the primordial embryonic germ cells through much of embryogenesis.
source: PIE-1 localizes prominently in nuclei in the early P-lineage blastomeres and persists in the primordial embryonic germ cells through much of embryogenesis (Mello et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The presence of PIE-1 correlates with global hypo-phosphorylation of the C-terminal domain (CTD) of RNA polymerase II (pol II) in germline blastomeres.
source: The presence of PIE-1 correlates with global hypo-phosphorylation of the C-terminal domain (CTD) of RNA polymerase II (pol II) in germline blastomeres (Seydoux and Dunn, 1997), and some studies suggest that PIE-1 may directly inhibit the CTD kinase to prevent transcriptional activation (Batchelder et al., 1999; Ghosh and Seydoux, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some studies suggest that PIE-1 may directly inhibit the CTD kinase to prevent transcriptional activation.
source: The presence of PIE-1 correlates with global hypo-phosphorylation of the C-terminal domain (CTD) of RNA polymerase II (pol II) in germline blastomeres (Seydoux and Dunn, 1997), and some studies suggest that PIE-1 may directly inhibit the CTD kinase to prevent transcriptional activation (Batchelder et al., 1999; Ghosh and Seydoux, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PIE-1 is a member of the tandem CCCH zinc finger protein family.
source: PIE-1 is a member of the tandem CCCH zinc finger protein family (Blackshear et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: PIE-1 differs from most of its homologs in having a prominent nuclear localization.
source: PIE-1 differs from most of its homologs in having a prominent nuclear localization.
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing feature of PIE-1 compared to other family members.

claim: PIE-1 localizes in the cytoplasm where it is thought to bind and regulate the expression of germline mRNAs, including the nos-2 mRNA.
source: However, like the majority of its family members, PIE-1 also localizes in the cytoplasm where it is thought to bind and regulate the expression of germline mRNAs, including the nos-2 mRNA (Tenenhaus et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A yeast two-hybrid screen identified the Krüppel-type zinc finger protein MEP-1 as a PIE-1 interacting factor.
source: Hints at the nuclear function of PIE-1 came from a yeast two-hybrid screen which identified the Krüppel-type zinc finger protein MEP-1 as a PIE-1 interacting factor (Unhavaithaya et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: MEP-1 co-purifies with LET-418, a homolog of mammalian ATP-dependent nucleosome remodeling factor Mi-2.
source: MEP-1 co-purifies with LET-418, a homolog of mammalian ATP-dependent nucleosome remodeling factor Mi-2 (von Zelewsky et al., 2000), and with HDA-1, a homolog of mammalian histone deacetylase HDAC1 (Shi and Mello, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MEP-1 co-purifies with HDA-1, a homolog of mammalian histone deacetylase HDAC1.
source: MEP-1 co-purifies with LET-418, a homolog of mammalian ATP-dependent nucleosome remodeling factor Mi-2 (von Zelewsky et al., 2000), and with HDA-1, a homolog of mammalian histone deacetylase HDAC1 (Shi and Mello, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Inactivation of maternal mep-1 and let-418 causes a striking developmental arrest of L1-stage larvae, whose somatic cells adopt germline-specific transcriptional programs.
source: Inactivation of maternal mep-1 and let-418 causes a striking developmental arrest of L1-stage larvae, whose somatic cells adopt germline-specific transcriptional programs, and assemble germline-specific peri-nuclear nuage-like structures called P granules (Unhavaithaya et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Inactivation of maternal mep-1 and let-418 causes somatic cells to assemble germline-specific peri-nuclear nuage-like structures called P granules.
source: Inactivation of maternal mep-1 and let-418 causes a striking developmental arrest of L1-stage larvae, whose somatic cells adopt germline-specific transcriptional programs, and assemble germline-specific peri-nuclear nuage-like structures called P granules (Unhavaithaya et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Soma-to-germline transformations in mep-1 and let-418 mutants depend on the trithorax-related protein MES-4 and components of a polycomb repressive complex (PRC2) (MES-2 and MES-3).
source: These soma-to-germline transformations depend on the trithorax-related protein MES-4 and components of a polycomb repressive complex (PRC2) (MES-2 and MES-3) (Unhavaithaya et al., 2002), whose functions are thought to promote fertility by maintaining germline chromatin (Strome and Updike, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MES-4, MES-2, and MES-3 functions are thought to promote fertility by maintaining germline chromatin.
source: These soma-to-germline transformations depend on the trithorax-related protein MES-4 and components of a polycomb repressive complex (PRC2) (MES-2 and MES-3) (Unhavaithaya et al., 2002), whose functions are thought to promote fertility by maintaining germline chromatin (Strome and Updike, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: PIE-1 functions as a master-regulator of the germline fate in C. elegans embryos, preventing somatic differentiation, while also protecting the germline chromatin from remodeling.
source: Taken together, these previous studies on PIE-1 suggest that it functions as a master-regulator of the germline fate in C. elegans embryos, preventing somatic differentiation, while also protecting the germline chromatin from remodeling.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple cited studies.

claim: The biochemical mechanisms through which PIE-1 exerts its dual effects on transcription and chromatin in the germline were entirely unknown prior to this study.
source: However, the possible biochemical mechanisms through which this small CCCH zinc finger protein exerts its dual effects on transcription and chromatin in the germline were entirely unknown.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: PIE-1 engages the highly conserved E2 SUMO ligase UBC-9 as shown by yeast two-hybrid screening.
source: By yeast two-hybrid screening, we show that PIE-1 engages the highly conserved E2 SUMO ligase UBC-9.
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: UBC-9 enzymes catalyze the addition SUMO to lysine residues on target proteins.
source: UBC-9 enzymes catalyze the addition SUMO to lysine residues on target proteins (Capili and Lima, 2007b; Geiss-Friedlander and Melchior, 2007; Johnson, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The reversible addition of SUMO (or SUMOylation) and its removal by de-SUMOylating enzymes is thought to occur on thousands of substrate proteins with diverse functions.
source: The reversible addition of SUMO (or SUMOylation) and its removal by de-SUMOylating enzymes is thought to occur on thousands of substrate proteins with diverse functions, especially nuclear functions including DNA replication, chromatin silencing, and the DNA damage response (Hendriks and Vertegaal, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: SUMOylation is not primarily associated with the turnover of its targets, but rather is often associated with changes in protein interactions.
source: SUMOylation can have multiple effects and is not primarily associated with the turnover of its targets, but rather is often associated with changes in protein interactions.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about SUMOylation.

claim: SUMOylation of a protein can promote interactions with proteins that contain SUMO-interacting motifs.
source: For example, SUMOylation of a protein can promote interactions with proteins that contain SUMO-interacting motifs (Matunis et al., 2006; Psakhye and Jentsch, 2012; Shen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The SUMO pathway promotes the activity of PIE-1 in preserving the embryonic germline.
source: Through a series of genetic and biochemical studies, we show that the SUMO pathway promotes the activity of PIE-1 in preserving the embryonic germline.
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 2.

claim: PIE-1 is itself modified by SUMO.
source: We show that PIE-1 is itself modified by SUMO.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: PIE-1 is not SUMOylated in early embryos, but rather in adult animals.
source: Paradoxically, PIE-1 is not SUMOylated in early embryos, but rather in adult animals where PIE-1 was not previously known to be expressed or functional.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data comparing embryo and adult lysates in Figure 1E and F.

claim: CRISPR-mediated GFP tagging of the endogenous pie-1 locus confirmed uniform nuclear expression of PIE-1 protein throughout the meiotic zone and in oocytes of adult hermaphrodites.
source: Indeed, CRISPR-mediated GFP tagging of the endogenous pie-1 locus confirmed uniform nuclear expression of PIE-1 protein throughout the meiotic zone and in oocytes of adult hermaphrodites.
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The type 1 HDAC, HDA-1, is modified by SUMO in a PIE-1-dependent manner as identified by whole proteome analysis.
source: Using whole proteome analysis for detecting SUMO-conjugated proteins, we identify the type 1 HDAC, HDA-1, as a protein modified by SUMO in a PIE-1-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry and western blot data shown in Figure 3.

claim: PIE-1 was originally thought to inhibit the MEP-1/Mi-2/HDA-1 complex in embryos.
source: Surprisingly, whereas PIE-1 was originally thought to inhibit the MEP-1/Mi-2/HDA-1 complex in embryos, we show that in the germline PIE-1 acts in concert with the SUMO pathway to promote the association of MEP-1 with HDA-1, and to maintain the hypoacetylation of germline chromatin.
evidence: This is stated as previous understanding that is being contrasted with new findings.

claim: In the germline PIE-1 acts in concert with the SUMO pathway to promote the association of MEP-1 with HDA-1.
source: Surprisingly, whereas PIE-1 was originally thought to inhibit the MEP-1/Mi-2/HDA-1 complex in embryos, we show that in the germline PIE-1 acts in concert with the SUMO pathway to promote the association of MEP-1 with HDA-1, and to maintain the hypoacetylation of germline chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4.

claim: PIE-1 acts in concert with the SUMO pathway to maintain the hypoacetylation of germline chromatin.
source: Surprisingly, whereas PIE-1 was originally thought to inhibit the MEP-1/Mi-2/HDA-1 complex in embryos, we show that in the germline PIE-1 acts in concert with the SUMO pathway to promote the association of MEP-1 with HDA-1, and to maintain the hypoacetylation of germline chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by H3K9Ac immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: pie-1 lysine 68 mutants that prevent PIE-1 SUMOylation are viable.
source: Although pie-1 lysine 68 mutants that prevent PIE-1 SUMOylation are viable, we show that they exhibit synthetic lethality in combination with null alleles of gei-17, a Drosophila Su(var)2–10 SUMO-E3 ligase homolog (Hari et al., 2001; Mohr and Boswell, 1999; Ninova et al., 2020), and that double mutants exhibit potent desilencing of a piRNA Argonaute sensor.
evidence: This is supported by brood size and embryonic lethality data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: pie-1 lysine 68 mutants exhibit synthetic lethality in combination with null alleles of gei-17.
source: Although pie-1 lysine 68 mutants that prevent PIE-1 SUMOylation are viable, we show that they exhibit synthetic lethality in combination with null alleles of gei-17, a Drosophila Su(var)2–10 SUMO-E3 ligase homolog (Hari et al., 2001; Mohr and Boswell, 1999; Ninova et al., 2020), and that double mutants exhibit potent desilencing of a piRNA Argonaute sensor.
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: pie-1[K68R]; gei-17 double mutants exhibit potent desilencing of a piRNA Argonaute sensor.
source: Although pie-1 lysine 68 mutants that prevent PIE-1 SUMOylation are viable, we show that they exhibit synthetic lethality in combination with null alleles of gei-17, a Drosophila Su(var)2–10 SUMO-E3 ligase homolog (Hari et al., 2001; Mohr and Boswell, 1999; Ninova et al., 2020), and that double mutants exhibit potent desilencing of a piRNA Argonaute sensor.
evidence: This is supported by piRNA sensor desilencing data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: PIE-1 engages SUMO to preserve the embryonic germline fate.
source: Our findings are consistent with a model in which PIE-1 engages SUMO to preserve the embryonic germline fate, and also to promote the assembly of a MEP-1/Mi-2/HDA-1 chromatin remodeling complex required for inherited Argonaute-mediated gene silencing in the adult hermaphrodite germline.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the collective findings of the study.

claim: PIE-1 engages SUMO to promote the assembly of a MEP-1/Mi-2/HDA-1 chromatin remodeling complex required for inherited Argonaute-mediated gene silencing in the adult hermaphrodite germline.
source: Our findings are consistent with a model in which PIE-1 engages SUMO to preserve the embryonic germline fate, and also to promote the assembly of a MEP-1/Mi-2/HDA-1 chromatin remodeling complex required for inherited Argonaute-mediated gene silencing in the adult hermaphrodite germline.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the collective findings of the study.

claim: A yeast two-hybrid screen identified SMO-1 (SUMO) as a PIE-1 interactor.
source: In addition, this screen identified the small ubiquitin-like modifier SMO-1 (SUMO); the E2 SUMO-conjugating enzyme UBC-9 (Jones et al., 2002); and GEI-17 (Holway et al., 2005; Kim and Michael, 2008), a homolog of vertebrate PIAS2 and Drosophila Su(var)2–10, an E3 SUMO ligase (Ninova et al., 2020; Pichler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: A yeast two-hybrid screen identified GEI-17 as a PIE-1 interactor.
source: In addition, this screen identified the small ubiquitin-like modifier SMO-1 (SUMO); the E2 SUMO-conjugating enzyme UBC-9 (Jones et al., 2002); and GEI-17 (Holway et al., 2005; Kim and Michael, 2008), a homolog of vertebrate PIAS2 and Drosophila Su(var)2–10, an E3 SUMO ligase (Ninova et al., 2020; Pichler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: GEI-17 is a homolog of vertebrate PIAS2 and Drosophila Su(var)2–10, an E3 SUMO ligase.
source: In addition, this screen identified the small ubiquitin-like modifier SMO-1 (SUMO); the E2 SUMO-conjugating enzyme UBC-9 (Jones et al., 2002); and GEI-17 (Holway et al., 2005; Kim and Michael, 2008), a homolog of vertebrate PIAS2 and Drosophila Su(var)2–10, an E3 SUMO ligase (Ninova et al., 2020; Pichler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PIE-1 contains a consensus SUMO acceptor motif (ψKXE) at lysine 68 that is conserved in PIE-1 orthologs of other Caenorhabditis species.
source: Motif analysis predicted one consensus SUMO acceptor site (ψKXE; Rodriguez et al., 2001) in PIE-1 that is perfectly conserved in PIE-1 orthologs of other Caenorhabditis species (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The addition of SUMO to substrates is rapidly reversible by SUMO protease enzymes that are active under conditions typically used to prepare lysates for immunoprecipitation studies.
source: Although covalent in nature, the addition of SUMO to substrates is rapidly reversible by SUMO protease enzymes that are active under conditions typically used to prepare lysates for immunoprecipitation studies (Di Bacco et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Preparation and centrifugation of lysates at 4°C followed by reconstitution in IP buffer resulted in the complete removal of SUMO from its target proteins.
source: For example, even the preparation and centrifugation of lysates at 4°C followed by reconstitution in IP buffer with no other incubation resulted in the complete removal of SUMO from its target proteins (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A poly-histidine epitope was inserted into the endogenous smo-1 gene to enable enrichment of SUMOylated proteins by nickel affinity chromatography.
source: To identify SUMO-conjugated proteins, we inserted a poly-histidine epitope into the endogenous smo-1 gene, and then used nickel (Ni) affinity chromatography under stringent denaturing conditions to enrich SUMOylated proteins (Tatham et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Editing the endogenous smo-1 locus to encode the L88K mutation caused a lethal smo-1 phenotype in C. elegans.
source: Unfortunately, editing the endogenous smo-1 locus to encode the L88K mutation caused a lethal smo-1 phenotype in C. elegans (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: Inserting in-frame FLAG or mCherry sequences into the endogenous smo-1 locus caused pronounced hypomorphic smo-1 phenotypes.
source: Inserting in-frame FLAG or mCherry sequences into the endogenous smo-1 locus caused pronounced hypomorphic smo-1 phenotypes (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: Inserting hexahistidine (HIS6) or decahistidine (HIS10) sequences directly after the initiator methionine codon of smo-1 resulted in fully viable and healthy strains indistinguishable from wild type.
source: We therefore inserted hexahistidine (HIS6) or decahistidine (HIS10) sequences directly after the initiator methionine codon of smo-1 without any other sequences. Both HIS fusions resulted in fully viable and healthy strains indistinguishable from wild type.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: The HIS10 fusion was chosen because it was robustly conjugated to target proteins and allowed better retention to the Ni-NTA resin under stringent denaturing and washing conditions.
source: We chose to use the HIS10 fusion because it was robustly conjugated to target proteins (Figure 1D) and allowed better retention to the Ni-NTA resin under stringent denaturing and washing conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B and C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Ni-NTA resin retains non-SUMOylated protein species that are recovered even in the absence of HIS10::SUMO expression.
source: The Ni-NTA resin retains non-SUMOylated protein species that are recovered even in the absence of HIS10::SUMO expression (e.g., see lanes 3 and 8 in Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Non-SUMOylated proteins are recovered via direct binding to the Ni-affinity matrix rather than via associations with SUMO-modified proteins.
source: These non-SUMOylated proteins are not recovered via associations with SUMO-modified proteins but rather directly due to background binding of the individual denatured protein to the Ni-affinity matrix.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: 977 candidate SUMO conjugates were identified by mass spectrometry analysis.
source: This analysis identified 977 candidate SUMO (Supplementary file 2; see Supplementary file 3, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, and Discussion section for comparison with previous studies).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: SUMOylated MRG-1 was strongly enriched by Ni-affinity chromatography as detected by MS and western blot analyses.
source: SUMOylated MRG-1, for example, was strongly enriched by Ni-affinity chromatography as detected by MS and western blot analyses (Supplementary file 2 and Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data and western blot data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: PIE-1 did not pass the arbitrary cut-off applied to the MS data for candidate SUMO conjugates.
source: PIE-1 did not pass the arbitrary cut-off we applied to our MS data (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: A FLAG epitope was inserted into the endogenous pie-1 gene to monitor PIE-1 SUMOylation.
source: We therefore carefully monitored PIE-1 SUMOylation by western blotting. To do so, we inserted a sequence encoding the FLAG epitope into the endogenous pie-1 gene.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used.

claim: The PIE-1::FLAG protein was expressed at similar levels in wild-type and his10::smo-1 worms, and these worms were fully viable.
source: The PIE-1::FLAG protein was expressed at similar levels in wild-type and his10::smo-1 worms (Figure 1E and F), and these worms were fully viable.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Ni-affinity chromatography of embryo lysates failed to enrich a modified form of PIE-1::FLAG.
source: Ni-affinity chromatography of embryo lysates failed to enrich a modified form of PIE-1::FLAG (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Ni-affinity chromatography of adult lysates enriched a slowly migrating form of PIE-1::FLAG protein that was ~12 kD larger than unmodified PIE-1::FLAG.
source: However, Ni-affinity chromatography of adult lysates enriched a slowly migrating form of PIE-1::FLAG protein that was ~12 kD larger than unmodified PIE-1::FLAG (compare lanes 14 and 19, Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The modified PIE-1::FLAG band was absent when the presumptive SUMO acceptor site lysine 68 was mutated to arginine in PIE-1::FLAG (K68R).
source: The modified PIE-1::FLAG band was absent when we mutated the presumptive SUMO acceptor site lysine 68 to arginine in PIE-1::FLAG (K68R) (Figure 1F, lane 20).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Lysine 68 is required for PIE-1 SUMOylation.
source: Thus, lysine 68 is required for PIE-1 SUMOylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the K68R mutation experiment.

claim: Previous studies had only detected PIE-1 protein within embryonic germ cells and proximal oocytes of adult hermaphrodites.
source: Previous studies had only detected PIE-1 protein within embryonic germ cells and proximal oocytes of adult hermaphrodites (Reese et al., 2000; Tenenhaus et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In embryonic germ cells, PIE-1::GFP localized to nuclei, cytoplasm, and cytoplasmic P granules.
source: As expected, in embryonic germ cells, PIE-1::GFP localized to nuclei, cytoplasm, and cytoplasmic P granules (i.e., P-lineage; Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Mello et al., 1996; Reese et al., 2000; Tenenhaus et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and citations to previous studies.

claim: In the adult pachytene germline, PIE-1::GFP co-localized with chromosomes.
source: In the adult pachytene germline, we found that PIE-1::GFP co-localized with chromosomes (as monitored by co-localization with mCherry histone H2B) and PIE-1 protein levels appeared to gradually increase during oocyte maturation (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: PIE-1 protein levels appeared to gradually increase during oocyte maturation.
source: In the adult pachytene germline, we found that PIE-1::GFP co-localized with chromosomes (as monitored by co-localization with mCherry histone H2B) and PIE-1 protein levels appeared to gradually increase during oocyte maturation (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: SUMOylation of PIE-1 occurs within the maternal germline.
source: These findings suggest that SUMOylation of PIE-1 occurs within a heretofore unexplored zone of PIE-1 expression within the maternal germline.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that PIE-1 is SUMOylated in adults but not embryos.

claim: Most homozygous PIE-1(K68R) animals produce viable and fertile progeny but exhibit reduced fertility and increased embryonic lethality.
source: By contrast, we found that most homozygous PIE-1(K68R) animals produce viable and fertile progeny but exhibit reduced fertility and increased embryonic lethality (Figure 2A and B), suggesting that the K68R lesion causes a partial loss of PIE-1 function.
evidence: This is supported by brood size and embryonic lethality data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The K68R lesion causes a partial loss of PIE-1 function.
source: By contrast, we found that most homozygous PIE-1(K68R) animals produce viable and fertile progeny but exhibit reduced fertility and increased embryonic lethality (Figure 2A and B), suggesting that the K68R lesion causes a partial loss of PIE-1 function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the phenotypic data.

claim: Placing the K68R allele over pie-1(zu154) dramatically enhanced the deficits in fertility.
source: Consistent with this idea, further lowering pie-1 activity by placing the K68R allele over pie-1(zu154) dramatically enhanced the deficits in fertility (Figure 2A) and in embryo viability (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by brood size and embryonic lethality data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: About 11% of embryos produced by pie-1(K68R)/pie-1(zu154) trans-heterozygotes failed to hatch.
source: For example, about 11% of embryos produced by trans-heterozygotes failed to hatch (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by embryonic lethality data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 64% (14/22) of dead embryos from pie-1(K68R)/pie-1(zu154) trans-heterozygotes arrested development with supernumerary intestinal cells.
source: When we examined a subset of the dead embryos by light microscopy, we found that 64% (14/22) arrested development with supernumerary intestinal cells, a hallmark of pie-1 loss of function (Mello et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy analysis and a citation to a previous study.

claim: PIE-1(K68R) exhibits a partial loss of PIE-1 function.
source: Thus, PIE-1(K68R) exhibits a partial loss of PIE-1 function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic complementation tests.

claim: RNAi targeting SUMO pathway factors (smo-1, gei-17, or ubc-9) caused wild-type and pie-1(zu154) heterozygous worms to make dead embryos.
source: RNAi targeting SUMO pathway factors (smo-1, gei-17, or ubc-9) caused wild-type and pie-1(zu154) heterozygous worms to make dead embryos.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Only 2–20% of embryos in the wild-type background made extra intestine when exposed to SUMO pathway RNAi, whereas about 75% of embryos made by the pie-1(zu154) heterozygous worms arrested with extra intestinal cells.
source: Whereas only 2–20% of embryos in the wild-type background made extra intestine, about 75% of embryos made by the pie-1(zu154) heterozygous worms arrested with extra intestinal cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: gei-17(RNAi) in wild-type worms caused only 20% embryonic lethality, whereas gei-17(RNAi) in pie-1/+ worms caused 82% of embryos to arrest development and 94% of these produced extra intestinal cells.
source: The synergy between gei-17 and pie-1(zu154) was particularly striking: whereas gei-17(RNAi) in wild-type worms caused only 20% embryonic lethality, gei-17(RNAi) in pie-1/+ worms caused 82% of embryos to arrest development and 94% of these produced extra intestinal cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A G56R amino acid substitution in ubc-9 resulted in worms that were viable and fertile at the permissive temperature of 15°C, but inviable when shifted to the non-permissive temperature of 25°C.
source: One allele, ubc-9(ne4446), which encodes a G56R amino acid substitution, resulted in worms that were viable and fertile at the permissive temperature of 15°C, but inviable when shifted to the non-permissive temperature of 25°C.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: Some of the temperature-sensitive phenotypes of ubc-9(ne4446) can be reversed by shifting worms back to the permissive temperature.
source: Some of the temperature-sensitive phenotypes of this allele can be reversed by shifting worms back to the permissive temperature (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: When shifted to 25°C beginning at the L4 stage, ubc-9(ne4446[G56R]) worms developed into fertile adults that produced 100% dead embryos (n = 332) with defective body morphology but well-differentiated tissues.
source: When shifted to 25°C beginning at the L4 stage, ubc-9(ne4446[G56R]) worms developed into fertile adults that produced 100% dead embryos (n = 332) with defective body morphology but well-differentiated tissues.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: About 15% of ubc-9(ne4446[G56R]) embryos arrested with extra intestinal cells.
source: About 15% of ubc-9(ne4446[G56R]) embryos arrested with extra intestinal cells, consistent with previous studies showing that in smo-1(RNAi) and ubc-9(RNAi) embryos, the P2 blastomere expresses EMS-like cell lineage patterns, a pie-1 mutant phenotype (Santella et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to a previous study.

claim: The proportion of arrested embryos with a pie-1-like phenotype was doubled when ubc-9(G56R) homozygotes were shifted to 25°C in a heterozygous pie-1(zu154)/+ background.
source: Strikingly, the proportion of arrested embryos with a pie-1-like phenotype was doubled when G56R homozygotes were shifted to 25°C in a heterozygous pie-1(zu154)/+ background (Figure 2F), supporting the idea that SUMO promotes the activity of PIE-1 in protecting the embryonic germline.
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: SUMO promotes the activity of PIE-1 in protecting the embryonic germline.
source: Strikingly, the proportion of arrested embryos with a pie-1-like phenotype was doubled when G56R homozygotes were shifted to 25°C in a heterozygous pie-1(zu154)/+ background (Figure 2F), supporting the idea that SUMO promotes the activity of PIE-1 in protecting the embryonic germline.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic interaction data.

claim: PIE-1 may recruit the SUMO machinery to regulate its targets.
source: The finding that PIE-1 interacts with UBC-9, SMO-1, and GEI-17 in the yeast two-hybrid assay (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1) raises the possibility that PIE-1 recruits the SUMO machinery to regulate its targets.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the yeast two-hybrid interaction data.

claim: 328 proteins were reduced to a similar extent in lysates from both pie-1(RNAi) and smo-1(RNAi) animals as revealed by Ni-affinity chromatography followed by MS.
source: Ni-affinity chromatography followed by MS revealed 328 proteins that were reduced to a similar extent in lysates from both pie-1(RNAi) and smo-1(RNAi) animals (orange dots in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3B and Supplementary file 4.

claim: HDA-1 is among the group of PIE-1-dependent SUMO targets.
source: Among this group of PIE-1-dependent SUMO targets, HDA-1 caught our attention because a previous study identified the nucleosome remodeling and deacetylase (NuRD) complex, including HDA-1/HDAC1 and its binding partners LET-418/Mi-2 and MEP-1, as potential targets of PIE-1 regulation (Unhavaithaya et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Slowly migrating isoforms of HDA-1 were present in adult his10::smo-1 lysates, but absent from embryo lysates.
source: Western blot analyses of eluates from Ni-affinity chromatography experiments revealed that slowly migrating isoforms of HDA-1 (Figure 3C, lanes 11 and 16) were present in adult his10::smo-1 lysates, but absent from embryo lysates (Figure 3C, lane 5).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Slowly migrating MEP-1 isoforms were present in both embryos and adults.
source: By contrast, slowly migrating MEP-1 isoforms were present in both embryos and adults (Figure 3D, lanes 5, 11, and 16).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The modified HDA-1 and MEP-1 isoforms were ~12 kD larger than unmodified HDA-1 and MEP-1.
source: These modified HDA-1 and MEP-1 isoforms were ~12 kD larger than unmodified HDA-1 and MEP-1, were only enriched by Ni-affinity chromatography of his10::smo-1 lysates, and were not detected in lysates prepared from smo-1(RNAi) worms (Figure 3C and D, lane 18), suggesting that the larger isoforms result from SUMOylation.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The modified HDA-1 and MEP-1 isoforms were only enriched by Ni-affinity chromatography of his10::smo-1 lysates.
source: These modified HDA-1 and MEP-1 isoforms were ~12 kD larger than unmodified HDA-1 and MEP-1, were only enriched by Ni-affinity chromatography of his10::smo-1 lysates, and were not detected in lysates prepared from smo-1(RNAi) worms (Figure 3C and D, lane 18), suggesting that the larger isoforms result from SUMOylation.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The modified HDA-1 and MEP-1 isoforms were not detected in lysates prepared from smo-1(RNAi) worms.
source: These modified HDA-1 and MEP-1 isoforms were ~12 kD larger than unmodified HDA-1 and MEP-1, were only enriched by Ni-affinity chromatography of his10::smo-1 lysates, and were not detected in lysates prepared from smo-1(RNAi) worms (Figure 3C and D, lane 18), suggesting that the larger isoforms result from SUMOylation.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The larger isoforms of HDA-1 and MEP-1 result from SUMOylation.
source: These modified HDA-1 and MEP-1 isoforms were ~12 kD larger than unmodified HDA-1 and MEP-1, were only enriched by Ni-affinity chromatography of his10::smo-1 lysates, and were not detected in lysates prepared from smo-1(RNAi) worms (Figure 3C and D, lane 18), suggesting that the larger isoforms result from SUMOylation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the western blot data.

claim: SUMOylated HDA-1 was not detected in extracts from pie-1(RNAi) adults.
source: SUMOylated HDA-1 was not detected in extracts from pie-1(RNAi) adults (Figure 3C, lane 17) and appeared reduced in adult extracts from homozygous mutant animals expressing PIE-1(K68R) (Figure 3C, compare lanes 11 and 12).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: SUMOylated HDA-1 appeared reduced in adult extracts from homozygous mutant animals expressing PIE-1(K68R).
source: SUMOylated HDA-1 was not detected in extracts from pie-1(RNAi) adults (Figure 3C, lane 17) and appeared reduced in adult extracts from homozygous mutant animals expressing PIE-1(K68R) (Figure 3C, compare lanes 11 and 12).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MEP-1 SUMOylation was unaffected by genetic perturbations of pie-1.
source: In contrast, MEP-1 SUMOylation was unaffected by genetic perturbations of pie-1 (Figure 3D, lanes 5, 12, and 17).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: SUMOylation of HDA-1 occurs only in adults and appears to depend—at least partly—on pie-1 activity and PIE-1 SUMOylation.
source: Thus, SUMOylation of HDA-1 occurs only in adults and appears to depend—at least partly—on pie-1 activity and PIE-1 SUMOylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the western blot data.

claim: In embryo extracts, where PIE-1 and HDA-1 are not modified by SUMO, MEP-1 interacted with both LET-418 and HDA-1.
source: In embryo extracts, where PIE-1 and HDA-1 are not modified by SUMO, MEP-1 interacted with both LET-418 and HDA-1 (Figure 4, lanes 10 and 11).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The robust interactions between MEP-1, LET-418, and HDA-1 in embryo extracts were not affected by the PIE-1(K68R) mutation.
source: These robust interactions were not affected by the PIE-1(K68R) mutation (Figure 4, lane 12).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In adult lysates, MEP-1 interacted robustly with LET-418, but only weakly with HDA-1.
source: In adult lysates, MEP-1 interacted robustly with LET-418, but only weakly with HDA-1 (Figure 4, lanes 22, 23, and 30).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The weak interaction between HDA-1 and MEP-1 in adult lysates was reproducibly detected, required both smo-1 and pie-1 activity, and was reduced in PIE-1(K68R) mutants.
source: Despite a co-migrating background band present in control IPs from animals without MEP-1::GTF (see Figure 4, lanes 7, 8, and 9 longer exposures), this weak interaction between HDA-1 and MEP-1 was reproducibly detected, required both smo-1 and pie-1 activity (Figure 4, lanes 31 and 32), and was reduced in PIE-1(K68R) mutants (Figure 4, lane 24).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4.

claim: SUMOylation of PIE-1 promotes a difficult to detect but reproducible interaction between HDA-1 and MEP-1 in the adult germline.
source: Thus, SUMOylation of PIE-1 promotes a difficult to detect but reproducible interaction between HDA-1 and MEP-1 in the adult germline, but is not required for their much more robustly detected interaction in embryos.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: SUMOylation of PIE-1 is not required for the interaction between HDA-1 and MEP-1 in embryos.
source: Thus, SUMOylation of PIE-1 promotes a difficult to detect but reproducible interaction between HDA-1 and MEP-1 in the adult germline, but is not required for their much more robustly detected interaction in embryos.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: If the interaction between HDA-1 and MEP-1 in adults requires the continued presence of HDA-1-SUMO, then IP assays would likely underestimate the in vivo levels of the protein complex.
source: Given the transient nature of the SUMO modification, it is worth noting that if the interaction between HDA-1 and MEP-1 in adults requires the continued presence of HDA-1-SUMO, then our IP assays would likely underestimate the in vivo levels of the protein complex (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a speculation about the limitations of the experimental approach.

claim: Immunostaining revealed increased levels of histone H3 lysine 9 acetylation (H3K9Ac) in pie-1 [K68R] gonads compared to wild-type gonads.
source: Indeed, immunostaining revealed increased levels of histone H3 lysine 9 acetylation (H3K9Ac) in pie-1 [K68R] gonads compared to wild-type gonads (Figure 5A and B), especially in the distal mitotic region and in oocytes.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: H3K9Ac levels were especially increased in the distal mitotic region and in oocytes of pie-1 [K68R] gonads.
source: Indeed, immunostaining revealed increased levels of histone H3 lysine 9 acetylation (H3K9Ac) in pie-1 [K68R] gonads compared to wild-type gonads (Figure 5A and B), especially in the distal mitotic region and in oocytes.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Exposing pie-1::degron::gfp animals to auxin from the L1 stage abolished PIE-1 expression in the adult germline.
source: Exposing these animals to auxin from the L1 stage abolished PIE-1 expression in the adult germline (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and caused a penetrant pie-1 maternal-effect embryonic lethal phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Exposing pie-1::degron::gfp animals to auxin from the L1 stage caused a penetrant pie-1 maternal-effect embryonic lethal phenotype.
source: Exposing these animals to auxin from the L1 stage abolished PIE-1 expression in the adult germline (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and caused a penetrant pie-1 maternal-effect embryonic lethal phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: Auxin-treated adult worms showed uniformly high levels of H3K9Ac throughout the germline.
source: Auxin-treated adult worms showed uniformly high levels of H3K9Ac throughout the germline (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: H3K9Ac levels were higher in oocytes of auxin-treated pie-1::degron::gfp worms than in oocytes of pie-1[K68R] worms.
source: Moreover, H3K9Ac levels were higher in oocytes of auxin-treated pie-1::degron::gfp worms than in oocytes of pie-1[K68R] worms (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PIE-1(K68R) is compromised (but not completely inactive) for its ability to promote deacetylation of H3K9 in the adult germline.
source: These findings suggest that PIE-1(K68R) is compromised (but not completely inactive) for its ability to promote deacetylation of H3K9 in the adult germline.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the H3K9Ac immunofluorescence data.

claim: pie-1(ne4303[K68R]) gonads exhibited mild changes in mRNA levels.
source: Whereas pie-1(ne4303[K68R]) gonads exhibited mild changes in mRNA levels (Figure 5C), a group of 479 genes were upregulated by more than twofold in pie-1::degron depleted gonads, as compared to wild type (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 479 genes were upregulated by more than twofold in pie-1::degron depleted gonads, as compared to wild type.
source: Whereas pie-1(ne4303[K68R]) gonads exhibited mild changes in mRNA levels (Figure 5C), a group of 479 genes were upregulated by more than twofold in pie-1::degron depleted gonads, as compared to wild type (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Upregulated protein-coding genes in pie-1::degron depleted gonads included many spermatogenesis-specific genes.
source: Upregulated protein-coding genes, included many spermatogenesis-specific genes (Figure 5E), suggesting that PIE-1 helps ensure a complete transition from spermatogenesis-specific gene expression to oogenesis-specific gene expression in the hermaphrodite.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: PIE-1 helps ensure a complete transition from spermatogenesis-specific gene expression to oogenesis-specific gene expression in the hermaphrodite.
source: Upregulated protein-coding genes, included many spermatogenesis-specific genes (Figure 5E), suggesting that PIE-1 helps ensure a complete transition from spermatogenesis-specific gene expression to oogenesis-specific gene expression in the hermaphrodite.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RNA-seq data.

claim: Five transposon families were upregulated in pie-1::degron depleted gonads, including Tc5 (256-fold) and MIRAGE1 (900-fold).
source: Five transposon families were upregulated (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), including Tc5 (256-fold) and MIRAGE1 (900-fold), suggesting that PIE-1 activity also promotes transposon silencing in the adult germline.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: PIE-1 activity promotes transposon silencing in the adult germline.
source: Five transposon families were upregulated (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), including Tc5 (256-fold) and MIRAGE1 (900-fold), suggesting that PIE-1 activity also promotes transposon silencing in the adult germline.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RNA-seq data.

claim: A comparison to adult gonad mRNAs upregulated in MEP-1-depleted animals and in animals homozygous for a putative HDA-1 SUMO acceptor mutant revealed a significant overlap, especially among spermatogenesis genes.
source: A comparison to adult gonad mRNAs upregulated in MEP-1-depleted animals and in animals homozygous for a putative HDA-1 SUMO acceptor mutant (Kim et al., 2021) revealed a significant overlap, especially among spermatogenesis genes (Figure 5F), suggesting that PIE-1 acts through the NuRD complex to regulate the majority of its adult germline targets.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data comparison shown in Figure 5F and a citation to a parallel study.

claim: PIE-1 acts through the NuRD complex to regulate the majority of its adult germline targets.
source: A comparison to adult gonad mRNAs upregulated in MEP-1-depleted animals and in animals homozygous for a putative HDA-1 SUMO acceptor mutant (Kim et al., 2021) revealed a significant overlap, especially among spermatogenesis genes (Figure 5F), suggesting that PIE-1 acts through the NuRD complex to regulate the majority of its adult germline targets.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RNA-seq data comparison.

claim: Mutations in smo-1 and ubc-9 activate germline expression of a piRNA pathway reporter.
source: In a parallel study exploring the role of SUMO and NuRD complex co-factors in piRNA-mediated silencing in the germline, we found that mutations in smo-1 and ubc-9 activate germline expression of a piRNA pathway reporter (Kim et al., 2021), but null alleles of gei-17 do not (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by piRNA sensor data and a citation to a parallel study.

claim: Null alleles of gei-17 do not activate germline expression of a piRNA pathway reporter.
source: In a parallel study exploring the role of SUMO and NuRD complex co-factors in piRNA-mediated silencing in the germline, we found that mutations in smo-1 and ubc-9 activate germline expression of a piRNA pathway reporter (Kim et al., 2021), but null alleles of gei-17 do not (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by piRNA sensor data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The piRNA sensor was desilenced in 67% of first-generation rde-3 homozygous worms and reached 100% in third-generation homozygotes.
source: The reporter was desilenced in 67% of first-generation rde-3 homozygous worms and reached 100% in third-generation homozygotes (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by piRNA sensor data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Two different pie-1 null alleles desilenced the piRNA sensor in 65% (15/23) and 54% (7/13) of first-generation homozygotes.
source: Two different pie-1 null alleles desilenced the piRNA sensor in 65% (15/23) and 54% (7/13) of first-generation homozygotes, but subsequent generations could not be monitored due to embryo lethality (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by piRNA sensor data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The pie-1[K68R] mutation had a mild desilencing effect: the piRNA sensor remained silenced in the first generation, but gradually became active over the next three generations, where it was expressed in ~50% of the fourth-generation homozygotes.
source: The pie-1[K68R] mutation had a mild desilencing effect: the piRNA sensor remained silenced in the first generation, but gradually became active over the next three generations, where it was expressed in ~50% of the fourth-generation homozygotes.
evidence: This is supported by piRNA sensor data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Two presumptive gei-17 null alleles failed to desilence the piRNA reporter through four generations of monitoring.
source: Two presumptive gei-17 null alleles failed to desilence the reporter through four generations of monitoring (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by piRNA sensor data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: gei-17/+; pie-1[K68R] hermaphrodites are completely sterile.
source: While attempting to make the gei-17; pie-1[K68R] double mutant, we found that gei-17/+; pie-1[K68R] hermaphrodites are completely sterile, suggesting that gei-17 is haploinsufficient in pie-1[K68R] mutants.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: gei-17 is haploinsufficient in pie-1[K68R] mutants.
source: While attempting to make the gei-17; pie-1[K68R] double mutant, we found that gei-17/+; pie-1[K68R] hermaphrodites are completely sterile, suggesting that gei-17 is haploinsufficient in pie-1[K68R] mutants.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the sterility of gei-17/+; pie-1[K68R] hermaphrodites.

claim: All 18 gei-17; pie-1[K68R] strains recovered exhibited complete first-generation desilencing of the piRNA sensor.
source: All 18 gei-17; pie-1[K68R] strains recovered in this way exhibited complete first-generation desilencing of the piRNA sensor (Figure 6B) and were also completely sterile.
evidence: This is supported by piRNA sensor data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: gei-17; pie-1[K68R] double mutants were completely sterile.
source: All 18 gei-17; pie-1[K68R] strains recovered in this way exhibited complete first-generation desilencing of the piRNA sensor (Figure 6B) and were also completely sterile.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result.

claim: Control injections into the otherwise wild-type piRNA sensor strain produced 10 homozygous gei-17 null strains that were fertile and viable but failed to desilence in the piRNA sensor.
source: In contrast, control injections into the otherwise wild-type piRNA sensor strain produced 10 homozygous gei-17 null strains that were fertile and viable but failed to desilence in the piRNA sensor (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by piRNA sensor data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: PIE-1 and GEI-17 appear to function redundantly to promote piRNA surveillance and fertility in the adult germline.
source: Thus PIE-1 and GEI-17 appear to function redundantly to promote piRNA surveillance and fertility in the adult germline.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic interaction data.

source: Here, we have shown that PIE-1 is also expressed in the adult germline where it does not directly inhibit transcription, but rather functions along with components of the SUMO pathway to promote the hypoacetylation of germline chromatin and with the SUMO E3 homolog GEI-17 to promote Piwi Argonuate-dependent gene silencing.

claim: PIE-1 functions along with components of the SUMO pathway to promote the hypoacetylation of germline chromatin.
source: Here, we have shown that PIE-1 is also expressed in the adult germline where it does not directly inhibit transcription, but rather functions along with components of the SUMO pathway to promote the hypoacetylation of germline chromatin and with the SUMO E3 homolog GEI-17 to promote Piwi Argonuate-dependent gene silencing.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: PIE-1 functions with the SUMO E3 homolog GEI-17 to promote Piwi Argonaute-dependent gene silencing.
source: Here, we have shown that PIE-1 is also expressed in the adult germline where it does not directly inhibit transcription, but rather functions along with components of the SUMO pathway to promote the hypoacetylation of germline chromatin and with the SUMO E3 homolog GEI-17 to promote Piwi Argonuate-dependent gene silencing.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Although PIE-1 is not SUMOylated in the embryo, genetic studies indicate that SUMO components, including the SUMO E3 ligase homolog GEI-17, function together with PIE-1 to preserve embryonic germline fates.
source: Although PIE-1 is not SUMOylated in the embryo, our genetic studies indicate that SUMO components, including the SUMO E3 ligase homolog GEI-17, function together with PIE-1 to preserve embryonic germline fates.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: PIE-1 interacts with SMO-1/SUMO and UBC-9, as well as GEI-17, by yeast two-hybrid.
source: PIE-1 interacts with SMO-1/SUMO and UBC-9, as well as GEI-17, by yeast two-hybrid, suggesting that PIE-1 may recruit these factors directly to its germline targets.
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PIE-1 may recruit SUMO pathway factors directly to its germline targets.
source: PIE-1 interacts with SMO-1/SUMO and UBC-9, as well as GEI-17, by yeast two-hybrid, suggesting that PIE-1 may recruit these factors directly to its germline targets.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the yeast two-hybrid interaction data.

claim: SUMO modifications to worm target proteins are rapidly and nearly completely reversed in IP sample buffer at 4°C.
source: We found that SUMO modifications to worm target proteins are rapidly and nearly completely reversed in IP sample buffer at 4°C.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: SUMO-dependent protein complexes are likely to rapidly disassemble and to thus be difficult or impossible to detect in co-IP studies.
source: Consequently, SUMO-dependent protein complexes are likely to rapidly disassemble and to thus be difficult or impossible to detect in co-IP studies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that SUMO modifications are rapidly reversed.

claim: The actual in vivo interaction between MEP-1 and HDA-1 in the adult germline may be much more robust than detected in co-IP studies.
source: Therefore, the actual in vivo interaction between MEP-1 and HDA-1 in the adult germline may be much more robust than detected here.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the labile nature of SUMO modifications.

claim: Appending a conjugation-defective SUMO by translational fusion to HDA-1 dramatically increased the association of HDA-1 with MEP-1 and other components of the NuRD complex.
source: This possibility is supported by parallel studies in which appending a conjugation-defective SUMO by translational fusion to HDA-1, HDA-1::SMO-1, dramatically increased the association of HDA-1 with MEP-1 and other components of the NuRD complex (Kim et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a parallel study.

claim: Studies in Drosophila identified a complex, termed MEC, where MEP-1 resides along with Mi-2, but notably, without HDAC.
source: Studies in Drosophila identified a complex, termed MEC, where MEP-1 resides along with Mi-2, but notably, without HDAC (Kunert et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The cultured cells where the MEC complex was identified were derived from ovarian tissues and express the Piwi Argonaute.
source: The cultured cells where this MEC complex was identified were derived from ovarian tissues and express the Piwi Argonaute (Mugat et al., 2020), raising the question of whether a parallel SUMO-regulated HDAC/MEC complex also functions in the Drosophila ovary but has been missed due to the labile nature of SUMO modifications.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A parallel SUMO-regulated HDAC/MEC complex may also function in the Drosophila ovary but has been missed due to the labile nature of SUMO modifications.
source: The cultured cells where this MEC complex was identified were derived from ovarian tissues and express the Piwi Argonaute (Mugat et al., 2020), raising the question of whether a parallel SUMO-regulated HDAC/MEC complex also functions in the Drosophila ovary but has been missed due to the labile nature of SUMO modifications.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings in C. elegans and previous studies in Drosophila.

claim: In the embryo HDA-1 is not SUMOylated and yet interacts robustly with its NuRD complex co-factors.
source: In the embryo HDA-1 is not SUMOylated and yet interacts robustly with its NuRD complex co-factors.

claim: SUMOylation of HDA-1 and other NuRD complex components may help overcome an unknown barrier to co-assembly in the adult germline.
source: Perhaps, SUMOylation of HDA-1 and other NuRD complex components helps overcome an unknown barrier to co-assembly in the adult germline, enabling the proteins to associate via a mechanism bridged by SUMO (Matunis et al., 2006; Psakhye and Jentsch, 2012; Pelisch et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of SUMO-dependent complex assembly.

claim: SUMO-dependent assembly could render the assembly and function of the adult germline NuRD complex more dynamic and responsive to signals that control the conjugation and removal of SUMO.

claim: SUMOylation of PIE-1 could enhance its E3 activity and its association with UBC-9 via the non-covalent SUMO-binding site on the backside of UBC-9.
source: SUMOyation of PIE-1 could enhance its E3 activity and its association with UBC-9 via the non-covalent SUMO-binding site on the backside of UBC-9 (Capili and Lima, 2007a).

claim: The N-terminal two-thirds of PIE-1—which includes lysine 68 and both zinc finger motifs—interacts with UBC-9 in yeast two-hybrid assays.
